title: The Cocoa Farm and the Offer

pages.text: Opanin Badu’s cocoa farm had fed his family for forty years. Tsatsu loved to walk its rows with his grandfather, looking up at the yellow and red pods. “Every tree is a promise,” said Opanin Badu. “We plant it, we wait, and one day it feeds us.” That Saturday, a stranger in a clean shirt stood at the edge of the farm with a folder.
sentences: Opanin Badu’s cocoa farm had fed his family for forty years.
Tsatsu loved to walk its rows with his grandfather, looking up at the yellow and red pods.
“Every tree is a promise,” said Opanin Badu.
“We plant it, we wait, and one day it feeds us.” That Saturday, a stranger in a clean shirt stood at the edge of the farm with a folder.
pages.alt: A grandfather and grandson walk between tall cocoa trees while a man in sunglasses waits by the fence.

pages.text: “I want to rent part of your land,” said the stranger. “Two machines and a few diggers, and in six months you will have more money than ten seasons of cocoa. Nobody will know.” He opened his folder and showed a roll of notes. Opanin Badu did not speak. He looked at the cedis, then at the trees. Tsatsu’s heart beat hard.

Nobody will know.” He opened his folder and showed a roll of notes.
Opanin Badu did not speak.
He looked at the cedis, then at the trees.
Tsatsu’s heart beat hard.
pages.alt: A stranger holds up a folder with notes while an old farmer looks at the trees.

pages.text: “Grandpa, let us count it,” said Tsatsu that evening. He got out his notebook. “If the offer is for one acre, how many cocoa trees are on an acre?” “About four hundred, if they are well spaced,” said Opanin Badu. “And how long do they bear pods?” “Thirty years or more,” said the old man. Tsatsu wrote: 400 trees, 30 years. “That is twelve thousand tree-years of cocoa,” he said.

He got out his notebook.

“And how long do they bear pods?” “Thirty years or more,” said the old man.
Tsatsu wrote: 400 trees, 30 years.
“That is twelve thousand tree-years of cocoa,” he said.
pages.alt: A notebook with sums, four hundred trees, thirty years, beside a candle and an old farmer’s hands.

pages.text: “Now the other side,” said Tsatsu. “Radio said that cocoa’s chief executive reported thirty thousand hectares of cocoa farms destroyed by illegal mining and other causes by December 2024, and fifty thousand more at risk. Other reports give lower figures, such as nineteen thousand. The numbers differ, but the farms are real.” “And when the diggers leave?” asked Opanin Badu. “A pit,” said Tsatsu, “and poisoned soil.”

Other reports give lower figures, such as nineteen thousand.
The numbers differ, but the farms are real.” “And when the diggers leave?” asked Opanin Badu.
“A pit,” said Tsatsu, “and poisoned soil.”
pages.alt: Two pictures: a green cocoa farm and the same land as a muddy pit with a lonely tree stump.

pages.text: “There is more,” said Tsatsu. “They say Japan and the European Union will test our cocoa for heavy metals. If our beans fail, buyers may refuse them, and every farmer in the area suffers. Cocoa supports about two million direct jobs, they say, and five million more indirectly. It is not just our farm. It is our road, our school, our market.” The old man closed his eyes.

pages.alt: A port with sacks of cocoa and a laboratory test tube, with a warning sign on one sack.

pages.text: “But Grandpa, I know why people say yes,” said Tsatsu. “Cocoa prices go up and down. A tree takes years to bear, and a single bad year can break a family. Some farmers have debts, sickness or school fees. Nobody is stupid for being tempted.” Opanin Badu nodded slowly. “Then the question is not only ‘should I?’,” he said. “It is also ‘what else can I do?’”

pages.text: The next day they visited the cocoa farmers’ co-operative and the chief’s palace. Opanin Badu asked for help with replanting, for the buyers’ price to be fair and for the Assembly to stop the diggers at the fence. He told his neighbours about the offer. Three of them said, “He asked me too.” Together they decided to report the stranger, and to ask the elders to protect the farms.

He told his neighbours about the offer.
Three of them said, “He asked me too.” Together they decided to report the stranger, and to ask the elders to protect the farms.
pages.alt: Farmers and elders talk together under a tree, with a large map of farm boundaries on the ground.

pages.text: Opanin Badu gave the stranger a polite but firm answer. “My farm is not for rent,” he said. “It is for my grandson, and for his grandson.” That evening, Tsatsu planted a new cocoa seedling in a gap between two old trees. “How long will this one take?” he asked. “Three to five years to bear,” said Opanin Badu. “Then you will be a man.” They both laughed. The end.
